points: Membrane: polytetrafluoroethylene, pore size 0.22 micrometres, area 0.014 square metres, direct contact configuration.
Conditions: feed temperature 65 degrees Celsius, permeate temperature 20 degrees Celsius, feed salinity 35 grams per litre, feed flow rate 1.5 litres per minute.
Initial permeate flux 18.4 kilograms per square metre per hour; polypropylene baseline module 15.9 under the same conditions.
Flux at the end of a 12 hour run 13.7 kilograms per square metre per hour, a decline of 25.5 percent from the initial value.
Deionised water rinse restored flux to 17.1 kilograms per square metre per hour.
Salt rejection 99.8 percent across the run, confirmed by ion chromatography.
definitions: membrane distillation = a thermally driven separation in which water vapour crosses a hydrophobic microporous membrane
permeate flux = the mass of permeate crossing unit membrane area per unit time
salt rejection = the share of feed salt that does not appear in the permeate, reported as a percentage
limits: Flux and rejection values hold for feed temperatures at or below 70 degrees Celsius and for a calcium-free feed; calcium sulfate scaling was not tested.
prose: Membrane distillation (a thermally driven separation in which water vapour crosses a hydrophobic microporous membrane) was applied to a saline feed in a direct contact module. The module held a polytetrafluoroethylene membrane with a pore size of 0.22 micrometres and an area of 0.014 square metres. Feed temperature was 65 degrees Celsius, permeate temperature was 20 degrees Celsius, and feed salinity was 35 grams per litre at a feed flow rate of 1.5 litres per minute. The feed circulated from a heated tank through the module and back to the tank, and permeate mass was collected on a balance at timed intervals for the flux calculation. Initial permeate flux (the mass of permeate crossing unit membrane area per unit time) reached 18.4 kilograms per square metre per hour (15.9 kilograms per square metre per hour for the polypropylene baseline module under the same conditions). A vapour pressure difference across the membrane drives the flux, and the difference is set by the two stream temperatures. Flux declined during 12 hours of continuous operation and reached 13.7 kilograms per square metre per hour at the end of the run, a decline of 25.5 percent from the initial value. The decline is consistent with partial wetting of the largest pores and with salt deposition at the membrane surface, and the two mechanisms act on the same timescale as the measured decline. A rinse with deionised water restored flux to 17.1 kilograms per square metre per hour, and the recovery after rinsing assigns most of the decline to deposition rather than to permanent wetting. Salt rejection stayed at 99.8 percent across the run, and ion chromatography of permeate samples confirmed the rejection from an independent route. Three membrane samples from a single production batch carried the full sequence of runs, and sample-to-sample variation in initial flux was small against the decline within a run. The flux and rejection values hold for feed temperatures at or below 70 degrees Celsius and for the calcium-free feed tested; scaling by calcium sulfate was not tested.

points: Biochar produced from wheat straw at a pyrolysis temperature of 550 degrees Celsius, with a carbon content of 68 percent.
Application rate 10 tonnes per hectare, mixed into the upper soil layer of a sandy loam.
Soil organic carbon rose from 1.12 percent to 1.47 percent after application, an increase of 0.35 percentage points and 31 percent relative to the unamended soil.
After an incubation of 180 days at field capacity, 87 percent of the added biochar carbon remained in the soil.

Cumulative carbon dioxide emission over the incubation was 214 milligrams per kilogram of soil for the amended soil against 246 milligrams per kilogram for the unamended soil, a reduction of 13 percent.
Soil pH rose by 0.4 units after application.
definitions: biochar = the carbon-rich solid remaining after pyrolysis of biomass in the absence of oxygen
soil organic carbon = the carbon held in soil organic matter, reported as a percentage of dry soil mass
pyrolysis = thermal decomposition of a material in the absence of oxygen
pH = the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity
limits: Retention and emission values hold for the single sandy loam tested and for incubation conditions; field ageing under rainfall and tillage was not measured.
prose: Biochar (the carbon-rich solid remaining after pyrolysis of biomass in the absence of oxygen) was produced from wheat straw at a pyrolysis temperature of 550 degrees Celsius and carried a carbon content of 68 percent. The biochar was ground, sieved, and mixed into the upper layer of a sandy loam in replicated pots. Application rate was 10 tonnes per hectare. Soil organic carbon (the carbon held in soil organic matter, as a percentage of dry soil mass) rose from 1.12 percent to 1.47 percent after application, an increase of 0.35 percentage points (31 percent relative to the unamended soil). The increase places a large share of the added carbon in the soil pool at the start of the incubation, and the retention measurement tests how much of that carbon remains. After an incubation of 180 days at field capacity, 87 percent of the added biochar carbon remained in the soil. Retention at this level is consistent with a condensed aromatic structure in the biochar, and the structure resists microbial attack over the incubation period. Cumulative carbon dioxide emission over the incubation was 214 milligrams per kilogram of soil for the amended soil (246 milligrams per kilogram for the unamended soil), a reduction of 13 percent. Lower emission from the amended soil held across the full incubation, and the difference grew during the early weeks, when labile carbon from the straw fraction is most available. Soil pH (the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity, reported in pH units) rose by 0.4 units after application, and the rise is consistent with the ash content of the straw biochar. Leaching losses from the pots were collected and carried a small share of the added carbon, and the retention figure excludes that share. The retention and emission values hold for the single sandy loam tested under incubation conditions; field ageing under rainfall and tillage was not measured.

points: Goal: obtain the wall shear stress for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe from a momentum balance on a cylindrical shell, with no empirical friction correlation.
Worked example inputs: pipe radius 0.05 metres, pipe length 40 metres, pressure drop 12 kilopascals over the length.
Balance result: wall shear stress is the pipe radius times the pressure drop divided by 2 times the pipe length, and the value is 7.5 pascals.
Check: the shear stress falls to zero at the pipe centreline and rises linearly with radius, and the integrated wall force matches the pressure force on the cross-section.
definitions: shell = a cylindrical layer of fluid at radius r with thickness delta r, concentric with the pipe
r = radial distance from the pipe centreline, in metres
shear stress = the tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals
wall shear stress = the shear stress at the pipe wall
limits: The balance assumes steady, fully developed laminar flow of a constant-density fluid in a straight horizontal pipe.
prose: This tutorial obtains the wall shear stress (the shear stress at the pipe wall) for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe from a momentum balance, with no friction correlation and no chart. The outcome is a single value from three inputs, and the same balance gives the shear stress at any radius as a by-product. A shell is a cylindrical layer of fluid at radius r (radial distance from the pipe centreline, in metres) with thickness delta r, concentric with the pipe. Take a shell of length equal to the pipe length and write the force balance on the shell in the flow direction. Pressure acts on the two annular end faces of the shell, and shear stress (the tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals) acts on the inner and outer cylindrical surfaces. The shell moves at constant speed, and the net force on the shell is zero. Set the pressure force on the shell equal to the difference of the shear forces on its two surfaces and divide by the surface area and the shell thickness. The balance gives the shear stress as a quantity that grows linearly with radius, from zero at the centreline to a maximum at the wall. Use the radius in the balance, not the diameter; a diameter in place of the radius doubles the result, and the error passes every unit check. Worked example inputs are a pipe radius of 0.05 metres, a pipe length of 40 metres, and a pressure drop of 12 kilopascals over the length. Wall shear stress is the pipe radius times the pressure drop divided by 2 times the pipe length, and the value is 7.5 pascals. The check is the limiting case: the balance returns zero stress at the centreline and the largest stress at the wall, and a profile with the maximum at the centre would signal a sign error in the pressure term. The result shows that wall shear stress in laminar pipe flow is fixed by the pressure drop and the pipe geometry alone, and the fluid viscosity sets the flow rate that the stress accompanies, not the stress.

points: Ammonia cracking supplies hydrogen at points of use where pipeline delivery is absent; the study tests a ruthenium catalyst on an alumina support for the reaction.
Reactor operated at 450 degrees Celsius and 5 bar, at a space velocity of 6000 per hour.
Ammonia conversion reached 96 percent, with a hydrogen output of 1.9 kilograms per day from the laboratory reactor.
Hydrogen purity after the separation stage was 99.9 percent.
A nickel catalyst reached 71 percent conversion under the same conditions.
Conversion fell by 1.8 percentage points over a run of 200 hours.
definitions: ammonia cracking = the decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen over a catalyst
conversion = the share of ammonia fed that reacts, as a percentage
space velocity = the volumetric feed rate divided by the catalyst bed volume
prose: Hydrogen supply at points of use depends on delivery by road or pipeline, and ammonia cracking (the decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen over a catalyst) offers storage and transport in a liquid carrier. The study tests a ruthenium catalyst on an alumina support for ammonia cracking in a fixed-bed reactor. The reactor operated at 450 degrees Celsius and 5 bar, at a space velocity (the volumetric feed rate divided by the catalyst bed volume) of 6000 per hour. The ruthenium catalyst cracked nearly all of the ammonia fed, and conversion (the share of ammonia fed that reacts) reached 96 percent, with a hydrogen output of 1.9 kilograms per day from the laboratory reactor. A nickel catalyst reached 71 percent conversion under the same conditions. Hydrogen purity after the separation stage was 99.9 percent, and the purity meets the feed specification for the fuel cell used in the test programme. Conversion fell by 1.8 percentage points over a run of 200 hours, and the fall was steady across the run. The conversion margin over the nickel catalyst places the ruthenium catalyst as the candidate for a field unit, and the stability result sets the first design question as catalyst life under start-stop operation.

points: The site stores 48 million tonnes of tailings from six decades of copper milling.
Original processing recovered 62 percent of the copper in the ore, and the unrecovered share reports to the tailings.
Tailings grade is 0.31 percent copper and 0.42 grams of gold per tonne.
The distribution of copper between oxide and sulfide minerals in the stored tailings is not known, and the distribution sets the choice between leaching routes.
The study maps the grade and the mineral distribution across the impoundment from 126 boreholes, and tests leaching on composite samples from each zone.
definitions: tailings = the ground rock residue discharged from a mill after extraction of the target metal
grade = the mass of a metal per unit mass of material, reported as a percentage or as grams per tonne
limits: The study covers one impoundment; the second impoundment at the site is excluded.
prose: The impoundment at the mine stores 48 million tonnes of tailings (the ground rock residue discharged from a mill after extraction of the target metal) from six decades of copper milling. Original processing recovered 62 percent of the copper in the ore, and the unrecovered share reports to the tailings. Tailings grade (the mass of a metal per unit mass of material) is 0.31 percent copper and 0.42 grams of gold per tonne, and grades at that level sit near the cut-off grades of operating mines with richer feed. Reprocessing of stored tailings is established practice at a small number of sites, and the published cases share a common feature: the mineralogy of the stored material was mapped before a route was chosen. The distribution of copper between oxide and sulfide minerals in the stored tailings at this site is not known, and the distribution sets the choice between leaching routes with different reagent demands and different residue behaviour. The study maps grade and mineral distribution across the impoundment and tests leaching response on composite samples from each zone. Sampling covers 126 boreholes on a grid across the impoundment, with assays and mineralogical counts on each core, and leaching tests follow the zones the mapping defines. The study covers one impoundment; the second impoundment at the site is excluded, and the exclusion bounds every grade average the study reports.

points: Silica particles with a nominal diameter of 200 nanometres were dispersed at 0.1 percent by mass in a potassium chloride solution of 10 millimoles per litre.
Dispersion pH was adjusted between 3 and 9 with dilute acid and base, and each dispersion rested for 120 seconds after adjustment before measurement.
Measurements ran at 25 degrees Celsius with an applied voltage of 60 volts across the cell.
A latex standard with a certified zeta potential of -42 millivolts read -41 millivolts at the start of each session.
Where a reading of the standard fell outside a band of 2 millivolts around the certified value, the cell was cleaned and the series repeated.
definitions: zeta potential = the electric potential at the slipping plane of a particle in a liquid, reported in millivolts, taken as a measure of the particle surface charge
electrophoretic light scattering = measurement of particle velocity in an applied electric field from the shift of scattered light
slipping plane = the boundary between the liquid layer that moves with the particle and the liquid that flows past
limits: The procedure covers aqueous dispersions of particles near the nominal diameter; concentrated dispersions and non-aqueous media are outside the procedure.
prose: Zeta potential (the electric potential at the slipping plane of a particle in a liquid, in millivolts) was measured by electrophoretic light scattering (particle velocity in an applied electric field, from the shift of scattered light). Silica particles with a nominal diameter of 200 nanometres were dispersed at 0.1 percent by mass in a potassium chloride solution of 10 millimoles per litre. Each dispersion was sonicated in a bath until no settled layer remained at the cell base, and the dispersion was used within the working day of preparation. Dispersion pH was adjusted between 3 and 9 with dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, and each dispersion rested for 120 seconds after adjustment before measurement. The slipping plane is the boundary between the liquid layer that moves with the particle and the liquid that flows past, and the reported potential is the potential at that plane. Measurements ran at 25 degrees Celsius with an applied voltage of 60 volts across the cell, and five readings were taken on each dispersion and averaged. A latex standard with a certified zeta potential of -42 millivolts read -41 millivolts at the start of each session, and the reading opened the measurement series for that session. Where a reading of the standard fell outside a band of 2 millivolts around the certified value, the cell was cleaned, the standard was remeasured, and the series was repeated from the first dispersion. Bubbles in the cell were cleared by tapping the cell wall before the series started, and a series with a visible bubble in the light path was discarded. Reported values are session means, and the spread of the five readings is reported with each mean. The procedure covers aqueous dispersions of particles near the nominal diameter; concentrated dispersions and non-aqueous media are outside the procedure.

points: The converter delivered a mean power of 38 kilowatts across the winter months of a 16 month trial, against a rated capacity of 200 kilowatts, a capacity factor of 19 percent.
Tank testing had predicted a mean power of 44 kilowatts for the same sea state distribution; the measured mean sits 14 percent below the prediction.
Availability was 91 percent of trial hours, with grid outages excluded from the availability count.
The device rode out a highest significant wave height of 6.8 metres with no structural damage.
definitions: wave energy converter = a device that converts the motion of sea waves into electrical power
capacity factor = the mean power over a period divided by the rated capacity, as a percentage
significant wave height = the mean height of the highest third of waves in a record
limits: The trial covers one sheltered site and one device; performance at exposed sites and array interactions are untested, and biofouling was cleared at each maintenance visit, so long-term fouling effects are outside the trial scope.
prose: The trial establishes the converter (a device that converts the motion of sea waves into electrical power) as a working generator at the tested site, with a mean power of 38 kilowatts across the winter months of a 16 month trial against a rated capacity of 200 kilowatts (a capacity factor, mean power divided by rated capacity, of 19 percent). Tank testing had predicted a mean power of 44 kilowatts for the same sea state distribution, and the measured mean sits 14 percent below the prediction, with the shortfall concentrated in the moderate sea states that dominate the site record. Energy forecasts for the site should carry the measured mean, not the tank prediction, until revised control settings are tested at sea. The shortfall assigns the main loss to the control settings at moderate wave heights, and the settings, not the structure, are the first revision the result supports. Availability was 91 percent of trial hours, with grid outages excluded from the availability count, and four maintenance visits cleared biofouling and replaced one mooring shackle. The device rode out a highest significant wave height (the mean height of the highest third of waves in a record) of 6.8 metres with no structural damage, and the survival case in the design basis is met at the tested site. The trial covers one sheltered site and one device. Performance at exposed sites and interactions in an array are untested. Biofouling was cleared at each maintenance visit, and long-term fouling effects stand outside the trial scope. A second device at an exposed site is the test the claim now requires.

points: Cell: alkaline water electrolysis, potassium hydroxide electrolyte at 30 percent by mass, temperature 60 degrees Celsius, electrode area 25 square centimetres.
Sweep: current density from zero to 800 milliamperes per square centimetre at a scan rate of 5 millivolts per second.
Cell voltage at the highest current density 1.87 volts for the coated anode against 2.14 volts for the uncoated anode.
Ohmic resistance from the high-frequency intercept 0.11 ohm square centimetres.
Curves are means of three cells; error bars are standard deviations, with a standard deviation of 0.03 volts at the highest current density.
definitions: polarization curve = the cell voltage plotted against current density for an electrochemical cell
current density = the current divided by the electrode area
figures: Fig. 1: polarization curve for a water electrolysis cell with a nickel-iron catalyst coating on the anode
prose: Fig. 1 | Polarization curve (cell voltage against current density) for an electrolysis cell with a nickel-iron coated anode, in potassium hydroxide electrolyte at 30 percent by mass and 60 degrees Celsius, with an electrode area of 25 square centimetres. The sweep reached a current density of 800 milliamperes per square centimetre at a scan rate of 5 millivolts per second. Cell voltage at the highest current density was 1.87 volts for the coated anode (2.14 volts for the uncoated anode), and the ohmic resistance from the high-frequency intercept was 0.11 ohm square centimetres. Curves are means of three cells; error bars are standard deviations, 0.03 volts at the highest current density.
